blocks.x: This is a real one Jim Robinson and we're at 808 Royal Street. Today is July what is it? 13th. Yeah July the 13th 1961. My name is Dick Allen so put your name on that too. Jim Robinson. Say it again? Jim Robinson. Okay. Okay now we'll sit back and relax. A lot of things to talk about. We're talking about Baton Rouge. You got up there a couple of years ago on a parade. What happened?

Oh that, you had to wash out. The Masonic parade. Four bands. That was a large parade. A bad day for it. The rain but that didn't stop the parade. People made the parade the day. After we all, sun come out and we got dry and came, got the bus and came on back home. What bands was that? It was the Tuxedo and the Ricker. It was a school band. Two school bands. I don't know the name of the school bands.
I see. So anyway, how do you like playing when the drums get wet? What does that do?

Well, you don't get no effect. You see, because the fella can't hit the drum too loud because they must bust the drum. You know, the head is wet and they'll bust the head. So I figure this way, when a parade like that, drums is the main thing in the parade, you know. When the drums go to drum is, you can't play the music like you want to play because the drums just keep the time. So when the head gets wet like that's the day you think, you might bust it at any minute.
Another thing we were talking about on the well here, not to mention names or anything, but what happens when you play with bad musicians? What does it do to you?

What I tell you, it takes, you mean with what musicians don't work together? You see, it feels that you, that you, you, you, you do another thing wrong, like I'm doing another thing wrong myself, understand? And I'm trying to do what's right. The other thing is, I know he's wrong, but you just can't say nothing to him, you know, but because otherwise, because you make hard feelings. So you got to just go and play like they play, you see. Then many people know that you can, that, that you can do better. Well, say, well, I went to play the other night, see Jim Routtson with such a group of fellas. Well, I'm going to play like they play. I can't go across the street up my lawns and different stuff and ruin my lips and different things just to make things sound smooth without trying to do my best. But now when I get to everybody, people can play and everybody can know what they're doing, well, I work that much more easy. And the other fellas work easy too. That's what I feel about it.
Well, suppose you take six guys that are strangers to each other, never met each other before, they're all star musicians. Can they play good together or not?

Well, now listen, it's a pain. Now if they're good musicians, and the first number they play, they can get together on that first number. They can get together on that first number. You see? You see? Because there's no question, because otherwise it's just like you see, you take the bands here. The fellas don't know how to rehearse, but especially get them on the street, they can play. You see? Your first number, you can get together. You understand? Your first number. There's no question. You can go and go play like you've been playing every day and every night.
But what's the difference between a jump up band and an organized band?

Well, it's a whole lot different. Because you see, an organized band, you see, every man knows his part, what he got to do. You see? And like if it comes to, or any number's got breaks and different stuff in it, you know, solos for, you know, some of the bars solo for trombone and the trumpet and the planet is harmonized. You understand why he got to own his solo. Maybe he plays some of the bars, then the trumpet. You see? See, that's, but that's, with an organized band, you see, because every man knows what he got to do. But you made a group that organized. It's like if I'm got a solo playing, well, I'm going to play by myself. What's up? Maybe I'm going to play two, three chords. You know, two, three chords. And then you've got to have fun and win. You'll get tired. But if you, if we're an organized band, and if I'm playing a chord, well that, that chord, they're going to, you know, play low rise under me. You understand? Push me along. You see? Anytime my lip get weak. That trumpet and that chord has really got the harmony going. You see? Mm-hmm. I'll let them get back and I'll just go ahead and finish my chords.
In other words, you help each other out. That's what the idea is.

You see, that's, that's where Joy and Lou's band had such a good reputation, good name, you see? Anytime when, uh, Kid Howard was playing at a, at a solo, me and George would play along with him, you understand? Every, anytime George had a solo, me and Howard would play along with George. And every time I had a solo, they'd play along with me. And after we, you think, we'd turn the rhythm loose, you see? You know? They'd play one or two chords, then we'd all come on in together, you understand? Music, all goes together.
So you'd kind of swap the lead around, huh? It's easy idea, and then everybody would keep working. I'd get the picture of them.

Well sure. You see, like, we made them records recording? You remember that chord we made? For who? For the, for the, what do you call it? This recording we made down at the Vance and Me Hall. This recording I made it. For Riverside. For Riverside. You saw my band, White Tip, on that recording? It wasn't no one man taking no four and five solos. You was there, wasn't it?
I was, sir. Well, I didn't miss the song to you. Well, that's the way I like it.

Did they sound for you? That's the way I like it, Jim. Well, that's Dixieland music. Dixieland music. But now, since they got this remarkable jazz, now the trumpet takes three or four chords, the tramo on three or four chords, the clarinet, understand? And all that was easy. It's not enough. If them things would, if them instruments would play along with the trumpet, understand? And, uh, that ain't gonna, that ain't, hurting you too much, understand? Not taking too much your, your breath, understand? Too much your wind. Just play along with the harmonized on them, you see? And that, when the pearls push me along, understand? You can do more. Up there by yourself. You can do more.
When did they start all the solo business down here?

Oh, well, when they started, first I heard it was in New York in 45. I went up at Bunk Johnson. I used to go over there by this fellow there, what you call him, the guitar player, what his name is? The one who has a nightclub up there? Yeah, right around the corner from us. What his name was? Eddie? Eddie Connors, yeah. He's a little bit around the corner from him. And that's where I heard the Wild Bill Davidson, because there was scooching every fellow, you understand? Solo. But the whole time we was up there, we never did do that.

You know, when I used to go up to Tyler's Big Auden in 1945, you weren't even here then, but you were in New York, I guess. I had Joe Avery and, and we were coming up there. I never heard a solo the whole time I was there. Not one solo. The trumpet would take down and that was all.

Well, and now, now I see, you're just switching to the truth. Now you take, now you take, but Lewis, Lewis Armstrong would tell you himself. The time that, when he was, when he was playing, when he was playing here. When he was at the Dixieland bands, there's no trumpet tape, no solo bar himself, or a clarinet, or a trombone. Sometimes the music would call for, sometimes three or four bars solo, something like that. Three or four bars. Some others would take it, you see. But now like, you play a solo, I take one, that's what I take one. But you see, all the bands play the way they want to play. But I figured, if the band harmonized together, at first, that's full all the vacant, full all the vacant with the music. Full it all up. You see. I see. The music sound better, you understand, when the whole band is ticking together. What's the smallest band you ever played with? The smallest band I've ever played with? I never played with a band over eight pieces. Especially the Dixieland band. The most, we played with, I played with six, or seven, six pieces, you know, eight pieces. When I was with Sam Morgan, we had eight pieces in our band, eight bands in our band. Did you ever play with just two pieces? Oh yeah, I didn't play many times. Just two pieces? Yeah, two pieces. Me and Kit Howard played many little, little parties, you know.
Really? What was Howard playing? Yes. Trumpet.

Trumpet and trombone and that's all? That's all. We played, we played in 55, Broadway, when Joyce took sick. We didn't have no, we didn't have no, we didn't have no trumpet. We did not have no, we didn't have no, we didn't have no, we didn't have no, we didn't have no, we didn't have no clinic. And Joyce took sick. And Lewis Alcombe come, that, that night even his wife was our guest. Mm-hmm. And Joyce played two numbers, they, two, three numbers, they took sick. And me and Howard played the whole dance with ourselves. Trombone, just trombone and trumpet. George again on banjo, Elton Paneil on piano, drag on bass, Joe on drum. Why did George take six? Well, George got overheated. He didn't understand. He played the whole night, the daughter read. Did you have a piano?

Oh yeah, we had a piano. He was playing that night. Yeah, he played piano. But I mean you played parties with just trumpet and trumpet on no rhythm? No, no rhythm. No rhythm. Well, how did you keep the beat going? Beat with your feet.
Beat with your feet? With your feet, yeah. Well, how did the people know what the beat

was? Well, people danced. They danced. They won't dance, yeah. What would Howard do when he got tired? Yeah, well I played. You'd play just trombone and nothing else. And the people could dance to that. Well, sure, sure. Yeah. Sure. Not many people have a beat like that, Jim, you know. That's one thing. Sure.

There'd be a bit of many. Many parties like that. What do you think about time in music? Time in music. Time in music. Now the time in music, understand, it's, it's, it's, it's, it's the drummer. The drummer won't keep. Yeah. The drummer, you see, it's all fall on the drummer. If you've got a good drummer. Mm-hmm. And, and, uh, you can't get away from him, understand, because he can hold you to time. You can try and cut loose what you want, but as long as he, hold you that time, you gotta come to him. The drummer can sell you, and the drummer can break you down. That's the drummer. That's the main thing of the band, a good drummer. Good, good rhythm, good banjo player, bass player. That's the main, that, and that piano player, that, that's the rhythm right there. The drum is, it's the thing to hold that time.
You like to play with the piano, or without one, which, if you had your cello. I, I love the piano.

You want a piano in your band? I love the piano, yeah. I love the piano and the band. I wouldn't feel the band. I love the piano because them, them things work together. Banjo, piano, and, uh, bass, drums, and things work together. You see, then there, there's a lot of, a lot of support for the men blowing the instrument, you see. When you got a good piano player and good banjo player and bass player, drum player, you can rest one or two, one or two chords, you see. Because they, because they, that, that, that, that rhythm's right there.
I suppose you want to cut one man out in the rhythm section. Suppose you only can use three. Which would you rather have?

What I tell you, every, I wouldn't want to cut no one, I think. I'm telling you the truth, because I feel, after, if the job was paying so much money, I figure, I wouldn't want to cut no, I'd rather, every man takes, take a cut off so much his, his money, and give the other problem, you see. We all get equal share. I figure that'd be fair enough.
Well, that used to happen in Magnet. I remember when I used to happen.
That'd be fair enough, you see. I, that's, I wouldn't want to listen to this.

throw a banjo player, a piano player, let's not say, well, we get the song so much, we cut, we break our saradon and get the same equal money that we get, understand? You see? That's keep your band together.

Well, you know, some people, they craft an after money proposition. But I feel every fellow got to live. And I wouldn't feel as a good man just for a few dollars. Well, I could figure out, say, well, the job paying $20, $30 a man, so what, we break the money down in the evening, understand? We get this equal share, and I think that's fair. We keep the band together.
Well, if you were going to pick out a band today, who would you pick to be in your band?

Oh, well, no, they got plenty of good musicians. I wouldn't want to say that, you see, because, you see, they got plenty of good musicians. I wouldn't want to say that. Because, I might say this, say something about this fellow, and something about that fellow, and so, and might get back to him again, and I wouldn't want to face nothing like that, because you got plenty of good musicians.

Well, I suppose, say, for all time, you know, any musician anywhere, living or dead, you can just choose the dead ones if you want to. Who would you pick? You mean for? Yes, all time, all star band. The best band for you.

Well, I tell you, like a band like we had, Sam Morgan band, we had a good band. You understand? We wasn't that, wasn't all that big, hard, hard, read for us, but what we played, everybody understand, and they liked it. They liked it, you see, and it comes with the time, we had the time, you see, we take a piece from, from, from, from no man way, and understand, we played and get it together and listen, we would make you dance off it. Sam was headed on time to it, and we played. We had good drummers, good band, good bass player, everything.

I don't know.
